The thermodynamic budget of objectivity
authors: Wonyong Chung
abstract: An event becomes a fact when enough independent records of it exist such that no operation is possible that leaves all observers ignorant of it again. Records are physical, and creating, keeping, and destroying them have thermodynamic costs. We compute these costs exactly in a minimal broadcast model with a driven central qubit writing records into $N$ initially thermal registers, with work sources and baths at temperature $T$. The basic arguments for the operations are outlined here, with full treatment in the text. Creation of one event record at redundancy $R$ and information deficit $δ$ requires work $W \ge R\, k_\mathrm{B}T \ln 2\, (1-δ) H(\varepsilon)$, linear in redundancy at the Landauer coefficient. Recording in a basis misaligned by $θ$ with the einselecting interaction fails at a critical angle, $θ_c = 2\arcsin\sqrt{H_2^{-1}(δ)}$, beyond which objectivity is unreachable at any work, and below $θ_c$ the optimal work is a closed form in the pointer basis that minimizes the work of objectivity. Reducing objectivity is impossible at any work with access to fewer than $R - R_{\min} + 1$ records, while work protects nothing if given access. Inter-record redundancy is extractable free energy and erasing the accessed records yields a net gain of work beyond the first copy. The second law constrains the destruction of the correlation: erasing a fact from a sector an adversary controls dissipates at least the mutual information erased, but a consolidation dissipates nothing. Records in re-thermalizing media are nonequilibrium steady states, and the minimal power to maintain a record at $(R,δ)$ is the known two-state driving bound evaluated at the record-quality boundary.

title: Linear Single-Source Shortest Path, Almost
LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
Complementary mechanisms of critical quantum metrology
authors: Nikita Leppenen, Shaked Levy, Ephraim Shahmoon
abstract: Critical metrology conventionally exploits enhanced susceptibility to a system parameter near a phase transition. Here we identify a complementary mechanism for critically enhanced estimation of intrinsic system parameters via suppressed quantum noise rather than enhanced response. We demonstrate both mechanisms in coherently radiating spin states (CRSS)-correlated states of $N$ spin-$1/2$ particles defined as asymptotic eigenstates of the collective-spin lowering operator with complex eigenvalue $r e^{-i\varphi}$. At the critical value $r=1$, CRSS exhibit a second-order transition. We show that near criticality, estimation of $r$ benefits from enhanced susceptibility despite increased noise, whereas estimation of $\varphi$ benefits from suppressed quantum noise without enhanced response. Remarkably, both yield the same estimation error $\sim N^{-2/3}$, improving over the standard quantum limit $N^{-1/2}$. For $\varphi$, this establishes quantum-enhanced metrology of phases intrinsic to the critical system, rather than phases externally encoded by interferometry. We demonstrate these results for CRSS realizations in both dissipative (superradiant) and Hamiltonian (Ising) systems relevant to cavity QED and trapped ions, where fast preparation of CRSS is shown possible thanks to gap opening. Applications to metrology of coupling rates and phases or optical lengths are discussed.

title: Monoidal analog of cluster-tilting theory and monoidal reachability of acyclic cluster algebras
Bound Entanglement with Negative Partial Transpose Exists
authors: Islam Faisal
abstract: We show that the Werner state $ρ= (23 I - 3\,\mathrm{SWAP})/1448$ on $\mathbb{C}^8 \otimes \mathbb{C}^8$ has a negative partial transpose and is bound entangled: no LOCC protocol can distill entanglement from any number of copies of $ρ$, and even with separable operations the fidelity of a two-qubit output with a Bell state never exceeds $(1+\sqrt{2})/4 \approx 0.604$. It follows that distillable entanglement is neither additive nor convex.

Transient entanglement generation in driven chiral networks beyond the secular approximation
authors: Yan Xi Foo, Kian Hwee Lim, Jia-Bin You, L. C. Kwek, Davit Aghamalyan
abstract: We study transient entanglement generation between two quantum nodes coupled through a chiral one-dimensional channel. In an emitter-only Born-Markov description, we show that continuous driving and an initial ground state can raise the maximum transient concurrence above the undriven 2/e benchmark associated with the effectively single-excitation model [1]. We then consider a more microscopic XX spin-chain channel with triangular plaquette couplings and compare a nonsecular time-convolutionless master equation (TCL-ME) with matrix-product-state (MPS) simulations. In the optimal driven regime, the nonsecular TCL-2 treatment reproduces the concurrence envelope and first transient peak qualitatively, while the remaining discrepancy is mainly attributable to beyond-Born system-bath correlations. The enhancement is traced to the failure of the secular approximation under strong driving, where nearby dressed transitions are not well separated on the dissipative timescale and nonsecular terms mix dressed-state coherences. Finally, we examine within TCL-2 the sensitivity of the protocol to positional disorder, imperfect chirality, and loss into nonguided modes. These results clarify when the familiar 2/e limitation ceases to apply and separate the roles of secular breakdown, Born-factorization error, and reduced-state memory in driven chiral entanglement generation; we believe that our study contributes in being one of the first studies where the breakdown of the secular approximation is useful rather than detrimental.

title: Statistics of time and frequency-averaged spectra in gravitational-wave background searches
Intelligent control of collisional architectures for multipartite Dicke-state preparation
authors: Duc Dung Vu, Minh Tam Nguyen, Özgür Esat Müstecaplıoğlu, Fatih Özaydin
abstract: Designing robust control protocols for multipartite entanglement is a central challenge for quantum technologies. We introduce a measurement-free collision-model protocol for preparing symmetric Dicke states | D n ( m ) ⟩ using excitation-preserving partial-SWAP interactions between two qubit registers and m shuttle qubits that remain part of the final state. The intra-register and shuttle–register collision strengths are treated as control parameters and optimized using a multi-start L-BFGS-B procedure. This extends collision-based entanglement generation beyond the single-excitation W-state sector without projective measurement or postselection. We assess the protocol under missed collisions, coherent crosstalk, independent and correlated dephasing, depolarization, and amplitude damping, and additionally quantify sensitivity to uncertainty in the assumed noise parameters. For the finite Dicke-state family studied here, optimized collision strengths preserve high preparation fidelities over broad imperfection ranges. These results provide a physically transparent framework for measurement-free Dicke-state preparation in repeated-interaction architectures.

title: Scalable spin squeezing in power-law-interacting X X Z models with disorder
authors: Samuel E. Begg, Bishal Ghosh, Chong Zu, Chuanwei Zhang, Michael Kolodrubetz
abstract: While spin squeezing has been traditionally considered in all-to-all interacting models, recent works have shown that it can also occur in systems with power-law interactions, enabling direct tests in Rydberg atoms, trapped ions, ultracold atoms, and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. For the latter, Wu et al. Nature 646 (2025) demonstrated that spin squeezing is heavily affected by positional disorder, reducing any capacity for a practical squeezing advantage, which requires scalability with the system size. In this Letter we explore the robustness of spin squeezing in two-dimensional lattices with a fraction of unoccupied lattice sites. Using semiclassical modeling, we demonstrate the existence of scalable squeezing in power-law interacting XXZ models up to a disorder threshold, above which it breaks down. We produce a phase diagram for scalable squeezing, and demonstrate the impact of critical slowing down close to the phase boundary. Our work is consistent with—and offers a plausible explanation for—the absence of scalable squeezing in the aforementioned NV experiment, while illustrating the maximum disorder allowed for realizing scalable spin squeezing in a host of quantum simulators. We highlight a regime with substantial disorder tolerance and identify controlled defect creation as a promising route for scalable squeezing in solid-state systems.

title: A room-temperature extreme high vacuum system for trapped-ion quantum information processing
authors: Lewis Hahn, Nikhil Kotibhaskar, Fabien Lefebvre, Sakshee Patil, Sainath Motlakunta, Mahmood Sabooni, Rajibul Islam
abstract: We present a room-temperature Extreme High Vacuum (XHV) system engineered to support the long-duration operation of a trapped-ion quantum processor. Background-gas collisions impose limitations on trapped-ion performance and scalability by interrupting algorithmic execution and, in some cases, ejecting ions from the trap. Using molecular-flow simulations, we optimize the chamber geometry, conductance pathways, and pumping configuration to maximize the effective pumping speed at the ion location. We perform high-temperature heat treatment of stainless steel vacuum components to achieve the desired outgassing rate, guided by quantitative relations of bulk diffusive processes, allowing us to reduce the H2 outgassing load to the 10−15 mbarls−1 cm−2 level. The final pressure in our chamber, measured by a hot cathode gauge, is 1.5 × 10−12 mbar, corresponding to the gauge’s measurement limit. We measure the local pressure at the ion location by observing collision-induced reordering events in a long ion chain of mixed-isotope Yb+. From the observed reordering frequency, we extract the average interval between collisions to be (1.4 ± 0.3) hrs/ion. This corresponds to a local pressure of (5.4 ± 1.1) × 10−12 mbar at the ion location, assuming that all collisions arise from background H2 molecules at room temperature. Our demonstration extends the continuous operation time of a quantum processor while maintaining the simplicity of a room-temperature system that does not require cryogenic apparatus.

title: Femicide in the Global Premodern
Orbit-Qubit Quantum Processor of Ultracold Atoms
authors: Ming-Gen He, Wei-Yong Zhang, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, Jian-Wei Pan
abstract: It is challenging to build scalable quantum processors capable of both parallel control and local operation. As a promising platform to overcome this challenge, optical lattices offer exceptional parallelism. However, it has been struggling with precise local operations due to relatively narrow lattice spacings. Here, we introduce a new quantum processor incorporating orbit-qubit encoding and internal states (as auxiliary degrees of freedom) to achieve spatially selective operations together with parallel control. With this processor, we generate one-dimensional and two-dimensional cluster states using minimal layers of controlled-Z gates. We experimentally detect the multipartite entanglement of a two-dimensional cluster state involving 123 orbit qubits through direct stabilizer measurements, verifying the full bipartite non-separability. Furthermore, we demonstrate measurement-based quantum computation by implementing single-qubit and two-qubit logical gates, highlighting the flexibility of orbit-qubit operations. Our results establish orbit-qubit optical lattices as a scalable quantum processing architecture, opening new pathways for quantum computation applications.

title: Detecting quantum phase transitions via shallow variational quantum circuits
authors: Ching-Yu Huang, Min-Fong Yang
abstract: Mapping quantum phase diagrams through classical simulation is notoriously resource-intensive, as even small systems far from the thermodynamic limit demand prohibitive computational effort. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) offers a compelling alternative, exploiting approximate ground states to distinguish phases. An appealing proposal, dubbed as Delta-VQE, determines critical points by contrasting variational energies optimized from reference states of distinct phases. Intriguingly, the diagnostic sharpens as circuit depth decreases, highlighting its promise as a resource-conscious probe of quantum criticality. To probe the broader applicability and underlying mechanisms of this approach, we investigate the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model with a three-spin cluster interaction, a setting in which the Ising transitions are generally situated beyond the self-dual line. We demonstrate that, whenever dual ansätze are employed, Delta-VQE invariably detects the self-dual points rather than the true criticality. In contrast, when ansätze are carefully tailored to embody the competing phases across the boundary, the genuine Ising critical point can be successfully identified with only minor finite-size effects. Our results establish that, while Delta-VQE provides a resource-efficient probe of quantum criticality without requiring precise ground-state preparation, its diagnostic power is fundamentally contingent upon the judicious selection of physically representative ansätze.

title: Multiplexed double-transmon coupler scheme in a scalable superconducting quantum processor
authors: Tianqi Cai, Chi-Tong Chen, Kunliang Bu, Sainan Huai, Xiaopei Yang, Zhiwen Zong, Yuan Li, Zhenxing Zhang
abstract: Precise control of superconducting qubits is essential for advancing quantum simulation and error correction. Transmon qubit systems employing the single-transmon coupler scheme have demonstrated high-fidelity gate operations by dynamically tuning the effective coupling between qubits. However, this scheme increases control-line count, posing a bottleneck for chip routing and scalability. To address this challenge, we propose a control-line multiplexing scheme based on a double-transmon coupler architecture, which enables shared coupler control lines to substantially reduce wiring complexity. We experimentally verify that this multiplexed configuration efficiently suppresses static Z Z coupling while maintaining accurate two-qubit gate control. We further demonstrate the feasibility of the architecture through two gate implementations: a fast coupler Z -control-based controlled- Z gate and a parametric iSWAP gate. To validate the practical applicability of this approach, we prepare Bell and three-qubit GHZ states with fidelities exceeding 99% and 96%, respectively. This architecture offers a route to reducing wiring overhead in two-dimensional qubit arrays, enhancing the scalability of superconducting quantum processors.

title: Exact gradients for linear optics with single photons
Efficient Targeting of Arbitrary Excited States with Quantum Inverse Power Iteration through Filtering Polynomials
An iterative Ising decoder for quantum error correction codes
authors: Yuanqi Liu, Weilei Zeng, Peixiang Li, Yantong Liu, Guangyao Huang, Yingwen Liu, Dongyang Wang, Junjie Wu
abstract: The Ising framework maps the decoding problem in quantum error correction onto ground-state optimization of a classical Hamiltonian, in which X – Z error correlations enter as cross terms. Under phenomenological depolarizing noise, the exact joint formulation contains up to 8-body interactions for the toric code and 10-body for the 6.6.6 color code. These high-order terms degrade solver convergence, inflate runtime, and raise the auxiliary spin overhead when embedding into native 2-body Ising hardware. In this work, we propose the iterative low-order decoding (ILOD) algorithm, which alternates between X - and Z -type sub-Hamiltonians, approximating cross-type correlations through Bayesian priors that reweight each type’s couplings using the other type’s inferred error configuration. This halves the maximum body count of interaction terms in the Hamiltonian, accelerating the solver, restoring convergence at larger code distances, and reducing the total spin count for 2-body embedding by a factor of 2.5. For the toric code, ILOD attains a threshold of 4.73 % versus 4.83 % for the joint formulation, with the empirical runtime ratio scaling as (0.81) d. For the 6.6.6 color code, the fitted ILOD and joint thresholds agree within statistical uncertainty, and ILOD remains convergent at larger distances where the joint formulation fails to converge despite a larger annealing budget.

title: Benchmarking and resource analysis for augmented-Lagrangian quantum Hamiltonian descent
authors: Zeguan Wu, Mingze Li, Muqing Zheng, Meng Wang, Junyu Liu, Samuel Stein, Ang Li, Yousu Chen
abstract: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) is a continuous optimization algorithm based on simulating a time-dependent quantum Hamiltonian whose potential energy encodes the objective function and whose kinetic energy promotes exploration through quantum interference and tunneling. While QHD is formulated for unconstrained optimization, many real-world optimization problems are constrained and highly nonconvex. In this paper, we benchmark AL-QHD, a hybrid framework that embeds QHD within the Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM), thereby solving a sequence of unconstrained subproblems while using ALM to enforce constraints. We evaluate AL-QHD on standard nonconvex test functions and use iterative refinement to improve solution accuracy at fixed per-run qubit cost. A finite-shot supplement replaces exact-probability feedback by measurement outcomes and scans 100–10,000 shots per readout, quantifying the empirical tradeoff between solution quality, reliability, and measurement cost across complete adaptive runs. Separately from the optimization benchmarks, we estimate gate-level resources for AL-QHD circuit constructions using ACOPF-derived symbolic models extracted from the synthetic Texas7k network dataset. These models contain 2–198 buses and 6–538 active variables and are used solely for resource estimation; we do not execute AL-QHD optimization on these models or solve the full Texas7k network. Resource estimates on Texas7k-derived ACOPF instances show steep hard-gate scaling, reaching ∼ 4.46 × 10 7 entangling gates in a NISQ-oriented model and ∼ 9.42 × 10 8 T gates in a fault-tolerant model at ∼ 5.3 × 10 2 active variables. These results suggest that AL-QHD is a useful framework for studying constrained nonconvex optimization with QHD, but that practical ACOPF-scale applications under the implementation analyzed here would likely require large-scale fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Sequential measurements as a resource in ancilla-assisted quantum metrology
authors: Koray Mentesoglu, Rahul Trivedi, Sara Mouradian
abstract: We present a protocol for simultaneous estimation of both quadratures of a displacement channel on a quantum harmonic oscillator using a single ancilla qubit, without complex state preparation or adaptive control. The qubit is coupled to the quantum harmonic oscillator via controlled displacements of strength A and undergoes N rounds of measurement and reset, while the oscillator coherently accumulates the displacement signal. Energy is injected and the non-commuting displacements imprint an order-dependent geometric phase at each round, giving a quantum Fisher information that scales as 𝒪 ( A 2 N 3 ) . Although the measurement record space grows as 2 N , we show that exact likelihoods for any individual measurement record can be computed in 𝒪 ( N 2 ) time. We show that measurement in the computational basis approximately saturates the quantum bound and maintains the 𝒪 ( A 2 N 3 ) scaling. Furthermore, the periodic information extraction makes the protocol robust to decoherence. Our results provide a framework for the design and analysis of sequential measurement in ancilla-assisted protocols.

title: Probing the Memory of a Superconducting Qubit Environment
authors: Nicolas Gosling, Denis Bénâtre, Paul Kugler, Simon Geisert, Nicolas Zapata, Mitchell Field, Sumeru Hazra, Simon Günzler
abstract: Achieving fault tolerance with superconducting quantum processors requires qubits to operate within the regime of threshold theorems based on the Born-Markov approximation. This approximation, which models dissipation as constant energy decay into a memoryless environment, breaks down when qubits couple to long-lived two-level systems (TLSs) that become polarized during operation and retain memory of past qubit states. Here, we show that non-Poissonian quantum jump traces carry the information required to distinguish long-lived TLSs from the standard Markovian bath. By fitting the Solomon equations to measured quantum jump dynamics arising naturally from thermal fluctuations, we can disentangle the qubit’s coupling to the two environments. Sweeping the qubit frequency reveals distinct peaks, each associated with a TLS that outlives the qubit, providing a handle to understand their microscopic origin.

title: A 3D stacked surface-code architecture for routing-efficient measurement-free quantum error correction
authors: Gunsik Min, IlKwon Sohn, Jun Heo
abstract: Mid-circuit measurement latency and noise can limit surface-code quantum error correction. Measurement-free quantum error correction (MFEC) replaces measurement and classical feed-forward with coherent feedback, but planar layouts then face a different bottleneck: inter-block transversal CNOT layers require SWAP routing with depth that grows as O(d). We propose a 3D stacked surface-code architecture in which vertically aligned couplers implement these CNOTs directly while stabilizer checks remain local within each layer. For the distance-3 rotated surface code, we provide an explicit embedding of transversal coupling, syndrome extraction, reset/copy, and single-target coherent feedback. For larger distances, effective-location extrapolations are used only to isolate the routing benefit, assuming a scalable coherent decoder. Under a superconducting-inspired decoherence model, the 3D layout becomes favorable when measurement-induced idling dominates coherent-operation errors. A sensitivity sweep with pvCNOT/p2q ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10} shows that a tenfold vertical-gate penalty weakens but does not remove the 3D advantage and increases the estimated break-even ratio by approximately 12–29%. A branch-level Pauli-frame check validates the distance-3 feedback grammar. The results identify vertical connectivity as a targeted architectural resource, while dense vertical-gate arrays and correlated inter-layer crosstalk remain open hardware challenges

title: Quantum algorithms for photoreactivity in cancer-targeted photosensitizers
authors: Yanbing Zhou, Pablo A. M. Casares, Diksha Dhawan, Ignacio Loaiza, Soran Jahangiri, Robert A. Lang, Juan Miguel Arrazola, Stepan Fomichev
abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a targeted cancer treatment that uses light-activated photosensitizers to generate reactive oxygen species that selectively destroy tumor cells, generally causing less collateral damage than conventional treatments. However, its clinical success hinges on the availability of photosensitizers with strong optical sensitivity and high efficiency in generating reactive oxygen species. While classical computational methods have provided useful insights into photosensitizer design, they struggle to scale and often lack the accuracy needed for these simulations. In this work, we show how fault-tolerant quantum algorithms can help identify promising photosensitizer candidates for PDT. First, we introduce a threshold projection algorithm that estimates the dipole strength within the therapeutic window as a measure of optical sensitivity. Second, we use the intersystem crossing (ISC) evolution-proxy approach to estimate electronic singlet–triplet mixing, with a separate vibronic dynamics treatment when nuclear motion must be included. We apply these algorithms to a clinically relevant and actively pursued class of photosensitizers, BODIPY derivatives, including heavy-atom and transition-metal-substituted systems that are challenging for classical methods. For active spaces of 11–45 spatial orbitals, we estimate 278–497 logical qubits for the qubitized implementations. Two readouts per execution reduce the absorption sampling cost at the same combined filtering and statistical accuracy. These algorithms directly evaluate photophysical quantities that can guide photosensitizer design.

title: A Qiskit-Based Simulation of Shor’s Algorithm
authors: Aarati Adhikari, Ram Krishna Tiwari, Harihar Paudyal
abstract: This study aims to explore the theoretical foundations and practical simulation of Shor’s algorithm, a quantum factoring algorithm technique that poses a considerable threat to classical cryptosystems, such as Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA). It has simulated the period finding process and the factorization of the integer N = 15 with base a = 7 by using Qiskit, a quantum computing framework. The quantum circuit correctly identified the period r = 4 from the modular exponentiation function 7x mod 15, leading to factors of 15 as 3 and 5. The simulation shows how quantum superposition, interference, and the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) were useful for speeding up the period-finding process, which is important for integer factorization. The histogram of measurement results revealed prominent peaks at 4, 8, and 12, which are multiples of the resultant period, unveiling the constructive interference produced by the QFT. However, a dominant peak at 0000 indicates hardware noise and error, pointing to the current limitations in quantum hardware. Fault-tolerant computers and error-correcting codes can overcome this limitation. As we move towards the age of quantum computers, the applicability of this algorithm poses a great threat to digital security. Applied code and visualizations provide a reproducible foundation for further study on cybersecurity and quantum computing.

title: Engineering Discrete Local Dynamics in Globally Driven Dual-Species Atom Arrays
Site-specific electric-field tuning of two-level system defects in superconducting qubit arrays
authors: Larry Chen, Kan-Heng Lee, C. H. Liu, Brian Marinelli, Ravi Naik, Ziqi Kang, Noah Goss, Sanchayeta R. Mudi
abstract: State-of-the-art superconducting quantum processors containing tens to hundreds of qubits have demonstrated the building blocks for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation. Nonetheless, a fundamental barrier to scaling further is the prevalence of fluctuating quantum two-level system (TLS) defects that can couple resonantly to qubits, causing excess decoherence and enhanced gate errors. Here we introduce a scalable architecture for local and in-situ electric-field tuning of TLS frequencies out of the spectral vicinity of our qubits. Our method combines TLS frequency tuning and universal single qubit control into a single on-chip control line per qubit. We demonstrate that we can independently control each qubit’s dissipative environment to map its individual TLS landscape and accordingly dynamically improve both qubit coherence times and single qubit gate fidelities with a constant time overhead that does not scale with the device size. Over a period of 40 hours across 6 qubits, we demonstrate a 36% improvement in average single qubit error rates and a 17% improvement in average energy relaxation times. Critically, we realize an 8-fold suppression in the occurrence of TLS-induced performance outliers, and a complete reduction of simultaneous outlier events. These results demonstrate a resource-efficient method to control TLS-qubit interactions, which can lead to an important route toward overcoming the challenges that TLS defects pose to scaling superconducting quantum processors.

title: Blockchain–Quantum Computing Integration for Smart City Pollution Management: A Comprehensive Framework for Multi-Pollutant Mitigation, Traceability, and Environmental Sustainability
authors: Dina A.M. Darwish
abstract: Rapid urbanization and industrial expansion have exacerbated multi-domain environmental degradation, encompassing greenhouse gas emissions, air particulate pollution, aquatic contamination, solid waste accumulation, and soil toxicity. Traditional environmental management systems suffer from centralized data vulnerabilities, severe computational bottlenecks in processing high-dimensional telemetry, and lack of immutable regulatory traceability. This manuscript presents a conceptual architecture and comprehensive narrative literature review exploring the theoretical integration of blockchain technology and quantum computing for smart city pollution management. Specifically, this study examines how decentralized cryptographic ledgers, quantum machine learning (QML), and quantum optimization algorithms can be coupled with 6G wireless communication infrastructures to automate real-time multi-pollutant mitigation. Furthermore, this work explicitly broadens the analysis of blockchain's established environmental applications—including pollution-data traceability, emissions monitoring, electronic waste tracking, supply-chain transparency, and regulatory compliance—while critically assessing how blockchain capabilities directly complement quantum computing in overcoming urban pollution challenges. The investigation is structured as a systematic narrative synthesis examining literature across databases including IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. The primary findings indicate that while quantum algorithms offer theoretical quadratic-to-exponential speedups for specific combinatorial optimization and molecular simulation problems under ideal fault-tolerant assumptions, current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware constraints necessitate hybrid classical-quantum workflows. Moreover, blockchain smart contracts combined with quantum-resistant lattice-based cryptography can secure environmental telemetry against emerging quantum decryption threats while providing immutable audit trails.

title: Reducibility of native weighted graphs on Rydberg arrays
authors: Johannes Kombe, J. D. Pritchard
abstract: We investigate the classical reducibility of random unit-disk graph (UDG) instances of the maximum independent set and maximum weighted independent set problems, which can be natively realized in Rydberg atom quantum processors. Using state-of-the-art kernelization techniques, we systematically probe how far classical preprocessing can simplify such native optimization problems of varying size and connectivity. While many small or sparse instances can be fully reduced, dense graphs often retain finite irreducible kernels even after extensive reductions. Introducing vertex weights tends to increase reducibility, whereas extending the interaction range in the underlying UDG connectivity suppresses the reduction efficiency. By exploring where classical reductions cease to be effective, we aim to delineate the regime of problem instances that remain computationally demanding—those most relevant for testing and benchmarking near-term quantum optimization hardware. We find that for the remaining finite kernels, quantum execution would require non-native embeddings with substantial resource overheads, suggesting that directly running native instances may be more practical than embedding a reduced kernel.

title: Adaptive memory-augmented Artificial Protozoa Optimization with competitive operator control for complex numerical and constrained problems
Adaptive GPU execution planning for memory-limited Hamiltonian applications
authors: Uriel Shafir, Ronnie Kosloff
abstract: Many quantum-simulation workflows, including propagation, filtering, Krylov, stochastic sampling, and observable measurement, are dominated by applications of Hamiltonians or other large operators, either to one state vector, ϕ=Ĥψ, or to several right-hand sides, Y=ĤX. These applications may be repeated many times, as in propagation and filtering, or may occur as one-shot observable, measurement, projection, or post-processing operations. The numerical algorithms used for these tasks are well established. The contribution of this work is an execution layer for these existing algorithms and operator evaluations when dense or effectively dense operator data exceed the memory of a single accelerator. The implementation first inspects the allocated hardware, including the number of GPUs (graphics processing units), available accelerator memory, and supported execution modes. It then enumerates candidate ways to apply the same mathematical operator: direct analytic action, seed-based generation, fused implicit kernels, on-demand block generation, parallel block execution, partial caching, full GPU caching, row-distributed caching across several GPUs, task parallelism, and hybrid row/task parallel execution. These candidates are ranked analytically using memory estimates, arithmetic-work estimates, cache requirements, and GPU-grouping constraints. The best analytically ranked candidates are then tested by a measured autotuner on the allocated hardware. Candidate comparisons use the same operator and input vectors and distinguish steady application time from calibration, compilation, cache construction, and tuning overhead. Plan selection minimizes expected total time for the declared number of operator uses. Validation against a fixed full-cache policy, direct GPU dense linear algebra, and a broader measured candidate search is used to quantify the benefit and overhead of adaptive planning. Logged trials may support learned ranking in future work, but no neural surrogate is used in the reported results.

title: Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality
authors: Shashwat Kumar, E. Rosenberg, A. Grajales Dau, Rodrigo G. Cortiñas, D. Maslov, R. Oliver, Adam Zalcman, M. Neeley
abstract: Quantum phenomena can be exploited to tackle certain problems beyond the reach of classical approaches. In this study, we focus on coordinated decision-making among many players without communication, the study of which, on current quantum processors, has remained elusive. Using a superconducting qubit processor, we show that quantum contextuality enables certain tasks to be performed with success probabilities beyond classical limits. With a few qubits, we illustrate quantum contextuality with the magic square game and quantify it through a Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality violation. To examine many-body contextuality, we implement the N-player Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger game and separately solve a two-dimensional hidden linear function problem, advancing the state of the art on fidelity and system size in both tasks. Our work introduces benchmarking of quantum processors using contextuality-based algorithms.

title: Performance comparison of QAOA mixers for ternary portfolio optimization
authors: Shintaro Yamamura, Satoshi Watanabe, Masaya Kunimi, Kazuhiro Saito, Tetsuro Nikuni
abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a quantum algorithm proposed for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices and is regarded as a promising approach to combinatorial optimization problems, with potential applications in the financial sector. In this study, we apply QAOA to the portfolio optimization problem, which is one of the central challenges in financial engineering. A portfolio consists of a combination of multiple assets, and the portfolio optimization problem aims to determine the optimal asset allocation by balancing expected return and risk. In the context of quantum optimization, portfolio optimization is often formulated using discrete variables. Unlike conventional binary formulations, we consider a ternary portfolio optimization problem that accounts for three states—holding, not holding, and short selling—and compare the performance of QAOA with different mixer operators and QWOA. For the XY-based mixers, we construct a uniform superposition over all constraint-satisfying ternary encodings to avoid the bias caused by simplified feasible initial states. Specifically, we implement QAOA with Standard Mixer, several XY Mixers (XY Ring, XY Parity Ring, XY Full, and QAMPA), and QWOA, and conduct simulations using real data based on the German stock index (DAX 30) for portfolios consisting of 5 and 8 assets. Furthermore, we introduce noise based on a depolarizing channel to investigate the behavior of QAOA with the Standard and XY-based mixers in realistic environments. The results show that, in the noiseless simulations considered here, highly connected XY-based mixers such as the XY Full Mixer and QAMPA generally achieve better performance than the Standard Mixer. However, their advantage is reduced in noisy environments, and the preferable mixer depends on both the QAOA depth and the noise strength.

title: The Differences and Connections between the Classical Jungian Model and Socionics: A Comparative Analysis
Adaptive log-Laguerre spectral method for the radial Dirac equation: Resolving asymptotic decay and core singularities in atomic calculations
Full-stack analog Gaussian optical quantum computing platform with one hundred inputs
authors: Shota Yokoyama, Atsushi Sakaguchi, Warit Asavanant, Kan Takase, Yi-Ru Chen, Hironari Nagayoshi, Jun-ichi Yoshikawa, Takahiro Kashiwazaki
abstract: Optical technology is a highly promising platform for quantum computing due to its enormous potential for large-scale, ultrafast computation. However, realizing a programmable and scalable system remains a significant challenge. Here, we present a high-speed programmable Gaussian quantum computing platform with one hundred inputs based on a continuous-variable full-stack architecture. Our system features a 100 MHz clock frequency and integrates a cloud-based interface with an open-source Python software development kit, mqc3, significantly enhancing accessibility and operational flexibility. We provide a comprehensive characterization of our system and its capabilities through multi-input and multi-step teleportation, as well as the programmable routing of quantum states across 101 input modes. This platform represents a critical milestone in scalable analog quantum information processing, offering a robust testbed for the future integration of non-Gaussian resources.

title: Tunable spectral correlations of highly multimode visible light via broadband quantum frequency conversion
authors: Federico Presutti, Logan G. Wright, Shi-Yuan Ma, Tianyu Wang, Benjamin K. Malia, Tatsuhiro Onodera, Peter L. McMahon
abstract: Multimode squeezed states of light are a resource for achieving quantum advantage in computing and sensing, where spatial or temporal modes have been the experimental norm. In our experiments, we generated highly frequency-multimode infrared quantum light and showed how adiabatic frequency conversion can be used to convert the quantum state to visible wavelengths while concurrently manipulating the joint spectrum by realizing a configurable many-port frequency-domain beamsplitter unitary transformation. We report near-unity efficiency quantum frequency conversion over a bandwidth >45 terahertz, which allowed us to measure the state with an electron-multiplying CCD (EMCCD) camera-based spectrometer, at noncryogenic temperatures. The parametric amplification and conversion of >400 frequency modes yielded an overall mean of ∼700 visible photons per shot and photon statistics consistent with squeezing. Our work shows how many-mode quantum states of light can be generated, manipulated, and measured with efficient use of hardware resources, motivating the use of frequency encoding in quantum optics.

title: C2 |Q⟩: A Robust Framework for Bridging Classical and Quantum Software Development
authors: Boshuai Ye, Arif Ali Khan, Teemu Pihkakoski, Peng Liang, Muhammad Azeem Akbar, Matti Silveri, Lauri Malmi
journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
abstract: Quantum Software Engineering (QSE) is emerging as a critical discipline to make quantum computing accessible to a broader developer community; however, most quantum development environments still require developers to engage with low-level details across the software stack—including problem encoding, circuit construction, algorithm configuration, hardware selection and result interpretation—making them difficult for classical software engineers to use. To bridge this gap, we present C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\), a hardware-agnostic quantum software development framework that translates specific types of classical specifications into quantum-executable programs while preserving methodological rigour. The framework applies modular software engineering principles by classifying the workflow into three core modules: an encoder that classifies problems, produces Quantum-Compatible Formats (QCFs) and constructs quantum circuits, a deployment module that generates circuits and recommends hardware based on fidelity, runtime and cost and a decoder that interprets quantum outputs into classical solutions. This architecture supports systematic evaluation across simulators and Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) quantum devices, remaining scalable to new problem classes and algorithms. In evaluation, the encoder module achieved a 93.8% completion rate, the hardware recommendation module consistently selected the appropriate quantum devices for workloads scaling up to 56 qubits. End-to-end experiments on 434 Python programs and 100 JSON problem instances demonstrate that the full C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\) workflow executes reliably on simulators and can be deployed successfully on representative real quantum hardware, with empirical runs limited to small- and medium-sized instances consistent with current NISQ capabilities. A proxy-based usability analysis further indicates substantial reductions in handwritten lines of code and explicit configuration steps compared to conventional quantum SDK workflows. These results indicate that C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\) lowers the entry barrier to quantum software development by providing a reproducible, extensible toolchain that connects classical specifications to quantum execution. The open source implementation of C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\) is available at https://github.com/C2-Q/C2Q and as a ready-to-use Python package at https://pypi.org/project/c2q-framework/.

title: Assessing Trade off between efficiency and Security Concern in AI adaption in Defense sector with India & Global Perspective
Quantum AI for Cancer Detection: Emerging Approaches in Intelligent Precision Oncology
authors: Syed Arshad Ali, Somya Priya Mishra, Swayam Bhatia
abstract: Cancer is the second biggest cause of death worldwide, killing nearly 10 million people annually with pancreatic, lung and colorectal cancer being the most prevalent cases, where patients are still diagnosed late in the disease process. In the past decade (2015-2024), the landscape of this picture has changed significantly: Deep learning architectures, notably convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have surpassed previous classifiers like support vector machines (SVMs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs) and are now nearing, and in some studies achieving, human diagnostic capabilities. More recently, the development of quantum machine learning (QML) and quantum neural networks (QNNs) has opened up yet another avenue for more detailed molecular simulation, quantum-enhanced liquid biopsies and AI-guided nano therapy. It summarizes over a dozen peer-reviewed research papers spanning that decade, from the classical machine learning era (2015-2018), to the deep learning surge (2019-2021), to the advent of hybrid quantum-AI systems (2022-2025), which is an area of quantum-AI-specific research that has increased by a factor of 10+ since 2015. The paper suggests a novel Quantum-AI Nano-Swimmer framework: a system comprising quantum biosensors, which can detect cancer biomarkers at the molecular level, and AI-guided nano robots, that have the potential to reach an accuracy of up to 99 percent when navigating the bloodstream to deliver targeted treatment. The paper concludes with key research gaps of the field and future research directions for the field in the near future, such as quantum drug discovery and the application of privacy-preserving federated learning for 2025–2030.

title: Resource-efficient digitized adiabatic quantum factorization
authors: Felip Pellicer, Juan José García‐Ripoll, Alan C. Santos
abstract: Digitized adiabatic quantum factorization is a hybrid algorithm that exploits the advantage of digitized quantum computers to implement efficient adiabatic algorithms for factorization through gate decompositions of analog evolutions. In this paper, we harness the flexibility of digitized computers to derive a digitized adiabatic algorithm able to reduce the gate-demanding costs of implementing factorization. To this end, we propose a new approach for adiabatic factorization by encoding the solution of the problem in the kernel subspace of the problem Hamiltonian, instead of using ground-state encoding considered in the standard adiabatic factorization proposed by Peng et al (2008 Phys. Rev. Lett. 101 220405). Our encoding enables the design of adiabatic factorization algorithms belonging to the class of quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) methods, instead the polynomial unconstrained binary optimization (PUBO) used by standard adiabatic factorization. We illustrate the performance of our QUBO algorithm by implementing the factorization of integers N up to 8 bits. The results demonstrate a substantial improvement over the PUBO formulation, both in terms of reduced circuit complexity and increased fidelity in identifying the correct solution.

title: Efficient color image encoding using chroma-subsampled hybrid quantum representation
authors: Vrushali Nikam, Manish Motghare, Reena Gupta, Vikas Panchal, Basudeb Dey, Smita M Nirkhi, Raiyaan Patel
abstract: Quantum image representation (QIR) is a fundamental component of quantum image processing, but existing color-image encoding approaches often require substantial qubit resources, gate counts, and circuit depths. This work presents CS-HQR (Chroma-Subsampled Hybrid Quantum Representation), a hybrid quantum classical framework that integrates YCbCr color space transformation and 4:2:0 chroma subsampling with quantum state preparation. The proposed framework preserves the luminance component at full spatial resolution while encoding chrominance components at reduced resolution, thereby reducing the amount of color information requiring quantum encoding. CS-HQR employs a dual circuit architecture in which the luminance component is encoded using 16 qubits and the subsampled chrominance components use 15 qubits including a channel selection qubit. The framework was evaluated using 6097 medical brain MRI images, with circuit level analysis performed across the complete dataset and reconstruction-quality analysis conducted on a representative subset. Compared with MCQI, CS-HQR requires 16 rather than 18 qubits and achieves approximately 54.0% reduction in transpiled gate count and 72.2% reduction in transpiled circuit depth, while maintaining high reconstruction quality. To assess generality beyond grayscale derived medical images, additional experiments were conducted on the Kodak, BSD500, and USC-SIPI natural colour benchmarks, obtaining mean SSIM values of 0.987, 0.981, and 0.984, respectively, with approximately 50% gate reduction. These results indicate that classical perceptual redundancy reduction can be incorporated into quantum image encoding to reduce state preparation resources while maintaining high reconstructed-image quality. The study provides a simulation-based evaluation of CS-HQR and establishes a basis for further investigation on hardware-aware and noise-resilient quantum image processing systems.

title: Geopolitical icebergs of the High North: the Arctic frontier of Nordic diplomacy
Quantum annealing for customer segmentation: a proof-of-concept QUBO framework for supply chain clustering
authors: Raphaël Bouchet, Alena Puchkova
abstract: This article investigates the potential of quantum clustering, specifically through quantum annealing, to enhance supply chain segmentation compared with classical K-Means. Using a proof-of-concept framework, clustering is translated into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimisation formulation, tested on customer datasets via both classical Simulated Annealing and D-Wave’s Leap hybrid solver, with penalty parameter optimisation introduced to address solver sensitivity. Performance is benchmarked against K-Means on runtime, accuracy metrics, and scalability, across dataset sizes from 200 to 5,000 points. Results show that while K-Means maintains superior inertia and stability, the hybrid quantum approach achieves faster solver-reported runtimes and, on a simplified 200-point, two-feature benchmark, delivers improved silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, and Dunn scores once penalties are optimised — metrics which, it is noted, reward the balanced partitions structurally favoured by the pairwise QUBO objective. However, scalability remains constrained by current qubit capacity and solver access, limiting practical deployment beyond mid-sized datasets. The study concludes that classical methods remain dominant for industrial-scale segmentation; the demonstrated framework, penalty-optimisation pipeline, and objective-level analysis nonetheless provide a documented foundation, grounded in a customer segmentation case study, upon which future quantum-assisted supply chain clustering can build as hardware matures.

title: Born-rule statistical dynamical quantum phase transitions under measurement
authors: Guan-Hua Chen, Guo-Yi Zhu
abstract: Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) occur at times when a quantum state exhibits a nonanalytic change in its return probability. This can be viewed as the probability of collapsing the evolved state to the initial state by quantum measurement. However, the initial wave function usually has exponentially small amplitude in the late time evolved state. Here, we perform statistical characterization of all the possible postmeasurement states distributed according to the Born rule, by sampling a one-dimensional quantum Ising chain after quantum quench dynamics. The statistical ensemble can also be viewed as a mixed state when the time evolved state is subjected to maximal dephasing noise in a certain basis. We map the distribution to a statistical model, and introduce its effective ``energy'' spectrum and the average dynamical free energy, establishing a framework for the statistical DQPTs. We show the recovery of the DQPT under high-moment averaging and a delocalized level distribution following critical times. Through analytic continuation into the complex time plane, we investigate the extension of Yang--Lee--Fisher zeros and the emergent level crossing near critical times. Finally, we propose a measurement-based quantum computation protocol to simulate the unitary evolution via single-qubit measurements on a two-dimensional cluster state. Our results provide a way to experimentally investigate statistical DQPTs in quantum devices, shedding light on the structured circuit sampling with insights from DQPT and generalizing the understanding of mixed states owing to decoherence beyond equilibrium.

title: Parameter-shift rules for gradients in boson sampling experiments
Quantum AI for road safety and beyond: A scoping review of applications in intelligent transportation systems
authors: Naima Goubraim, Zouhair Elamrani Abou Elassad, Hajar Ouhmidou, Hajar Mousannif
abstract: Background Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) increasingly draw on artificial intelligence for prediction, classification, and control tasks. Quantum computing and quantum machine learning (QML) have emerged as candidate tools, though current hardware remains in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. Objective This review maps the literature applying quantum or quantum-inspired AI to ITS, with attention to road-safety applications. Methods A PRISMA-ScR-adapted scoping review searched five databases (Web of Science, ScienceDirect, arXiv, Scopus, IEEE Xplore). Screening was conducted jointly by the review author and a co-author against structured eligibility criteria; an independent, criteria-blind AI-assisted second pass assessed reliability (substantial agreement, kappa = 0.77). From 271 records identified, 50 were synthesized: 41 primary studies and 9 background reviews. A five-item quality checklist was applied to the 15 primary studies with confirmed full-text access. Results The 41 primary studies span five application themes, led by collision/accident detection and avoidance (22 studies), ahead of traffic-state forecasting, ITS operations, electric-vehicle systems, and network security. Reported methods include quantum neural networks, support vector machines, variational circuits, game theory, annealing/QAOA, and federated learning. Quantum and hybrid approaches outperformed classical baselines on structured, interaction-heavy tasks using markedly fewer parameters, though fixed quantum-kernel methods showed recurring overfitting; most studies ran on simulators rather than physical hardware. Conclusion Quantum AI for ITS is a young, rapidly growing field (mostly 2024–2026) in which road safety is the largest application cluster. Reported advantage centers on parameter efficiency, not raw accuracy. Key gaps include near-absent physical-hardware validation, standardized benchmarks, and fully independent dual screening.

title: Improved Join Order Optimization for Database Queries Using Hybrid Quantum-Classical Approaches for QUBO Problems
authors: Nitin Nayak, Sven Groppe, Tobias Winker, Umut Çalıkyılmaz, Jinghua Groppe
abstract: Efficient query optimization is crucial for relational database systems, especially for optimizing join orders in complex queries. This work introduces a hybrid approach that integrates Eliminating Cartesian Products (ECP) with splitting the QUBO search space (SQSS) to reduce the size of the QUBO problem, minimizing binary variables and constraints. This improves the performance of the quantum algorithm while lowering hardware requirements. We evaluate our method using real-world SQL queries from the ErgastF1 dataset on quantum and classical algorithms, including Quantum Annealing (QA), Simulated Annealing (SA), QAOA, and VQE, implemented on D-Wave’s Quantum Annealer and universal gate-based simulators. Additionally, we analyze the impact of selectivity and SQSS on QUBO weight distribution and algorithmic performance, highlighting optimization efficiency for QA and SA. Experimental results show consistent optimal join orders and enhanced query optimization for various selectivity conditions, and it also highlights the limitations of current quantum hardware for complex queries. This study further confirms the potential of hybrid quantum-classical methods for scalable quantum-enhanced database optimization.

title: Quantum Computing in the NISQ Era: A Scientometric Mapping of Research Trends, Hotspots, and Emerging Frontiers (2018-2025)
authors: Mahadevaswamy Shanthamallappa, Pradeep Kumar Benakanahalli Puttappa
abstract: In recent years, quantum computing has gained more and more of a research interest, especially with the emergence of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems. This study is a bibliometric analysis of the publications related to NISQ quantum computing from 2018 to 2025. Publications were pulled from the OpenAlex database and narrowed down by the relevance of the records to NISQ related quantum computing. A total of 2,524 publications were selected for the final analysis. The study covers the growth of publications, citation characteristics, main research areas, research hotspots, leading contributors, geographic distribution and new research areas. The results indicate that the publishing activity has been significantly rising, peaking in 2022-2023. Based on the thematic analysis, the key directions for NISQ research are found to be quantum algorithms, variational quantum methods, quantum machine learning, quantum hardware, optimization, and error control. The analysis also indicates that there is greater thematic variety, indicating that NISQ research has diversified to a number of related fields. The United States is the primary source, followed by China, the United Kingdom and various major universities and research institutions. The citation maturity indicates that more mature citation is seen in the older publications, while newer publications are still building up their level of citations. The 2025 research snapshot also shows that there are strong linkages between the fields of quantum computing, computer science, physics, mathematics, optimization, and AI. The study gives a structured insight into the development and evolution of the research interest in NISQ quantum computing, and identifies areas that will likely continue to be the focus of research.

title: Advanced semiconductor materials for future electronic systems: from conventional to quantum devices
authors: Ali Ahmed Alqudaihi, N. Dhasarathan, Amaleswari Rajulapati, Vijayakumar Sivasundar, Akanksha Mishra, Santosh Kumar Sahu, Ravi Kumar V., Mohammed Aman
abstract: Modern electronics have advanced through the continuous improvement of semiconductor technology. However, the fundamental limitations of conventional silicon, including scaling constraints, short-channel effects, and quantum phenomena, necessitate advanced semiconductor materials and next-generation device architectures. This review discusses the development of semiconductor materials from conventional elemental and compound semiconductors to wide-band-gap, two-dimensional (2D), organic, and quantum semiconductors for future electronic systems. It covers semiconductor physics, band structure engineering, material characterization, device performance metrics, and recent advances in crystal growth, epitaxial growth, film deposition, nanofabrication, and doping techniques. This review also examines emerging semiconductor devices, including FinFETs, gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, neuromorphic and memristive devices, spintronics, and quantum semiconductor devices. Atomically thin 2D semiconductors offer remarkable electrostatic control for future miniaturization, while wide-band-gap semiconductors provide higher breakdown field strength and stability than silicon. Furthermore, the review evaluates defect engineering, interface reliability, quantum–material quality, heterogeneous integration, and fabrication compatibility, particularly the BEOL thermal budget below 400 °C, which is critical for integrating new semiconductor channels with silicon logic. Consequently, low-temperature deposition processes such as atomic layer deposition (ALD), plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD), and selective CVD/MOCVD methods provide beneficial routes for heterogeneous integration.

title: Implicit differentiation for measurement-efficient bilevel quantum-classical optimization
authors: Tobias Rohe, Markus Baumann, Federico Harjes Ruiloba, Maximilian Zorn, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff–Popien
journal: Frontiers in Quantum Science and Technology
abstract: Quantum optimization has shown promising results for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems. Real-world applications, however, often involve polynomial coefficients that depend on tunable external factors—such as demand forecasts or risk preferences—giving rise to bilevel optimization structures. We show how variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) can efficiently handle such parametric problems, thus making three contributions. First, we propose a bilevel optimization model for diagonal cost Hamiltonians where coefficients depend on a tunable outer parameter: an outer loop adjusts this parameter—reshaping the cost landscape—while an inner VQA optimizes circuit variables. Second, since derivative-free probing methods incur multiplicative overhead when each outer evaluation requires a complete inner solve, we develop correlator-reuse implicit differentiation (CR-ID), which obtains outer gradients by reusing quantum measurements already collected during inner energy estimation, thus requiring essentially no additional circuit executions. Experiments across three coefficient families show that CR-ID consistently improves budget-normalized efficiency by 4% in 1D and over 14% in multi-dimensional settings, showing a significant performance advantage compared to finite-difference methods. Third, we show that this property is architecture-dependent: the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) admits exact reuse gradients, whereas the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) introduces a state-dependent term that creates a cost–bias trade-off.

title: Fully quantum algorithmic framework for partial differential equation-constrained optimization
authors: Yuki Sato, Jumpei Kato, Hiroshi Yano, Kosuke Ito, Naoki Yamamoto
abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE)-constrained optimization, where an optimization problem is subject to PDE constraints, arises in various applications such as design, control, and inference. Solving such problems is computationally demanding because it requires repeatedly solving a PDE and using its solution within an optimization process. In this paper, we first propose a fully quantum algorithmic framework for solving PDE-constrained optimization problems. The proposed method combines a quantum PDE solver that prepares the solution vector as a quantum state, and a quantum optimizer that assumes oracle access to a quantized objective function. The central idea is the explicit construction of the oracle in a form of block-encoding for the objective function, which coherently uses the output of a quantum PDE solver. This enables us to avoid classical access to the full solution that requires quantum state tomography canceling out the potential quantum speedups. We also derive the overall computational complexity of the proposed method with respect to parameters for optimization and PDE simulation, where quantum speedup is inherited from the underlying quantum PDE solver. We numerically demonstrate the validity of the proposed method by applications, including a parameter calibration problem in the Black-Scholes equation and a material parameter design problem in the wave equation. This work presents the concept of composing quantum subroutines so that the weakness of one (i.e., prohibitive readout overhead) is neutralized by the strength of another (i.e., coherent oracle access), toward a bottleneck-free quantum algorithm.

title: Quantum Forensics in Cybercrime Investigation and Digital Forensics: From Digital Footprints to Strategic Decision-Making
Advances in Quantum Technology: A Comprehensive Survey of Hardware Platforms, Quantum Algorithms, Error Correction, Cryptography, and Emerging Applications Across the Quantum Computing Ecosystem
authors: Korra Srinivas, V Anil Santhosh, E.Gurumoorthi, B Giridhar, K.Aarathi
abstract: The move from lab demonstrations to designed quantum technology is underway, but the development in hardware, algorithms, error correction and safe communication is uneven. The survey is comprehensive, covering the full stack: superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic, silicon-spin and topological qubits; Shor, Grover, HHL, VQE, QAOA and quantum machine learning; stabilizer and surface-code error correction; quantum key distribution and post-quantum cryptography; and applications in chemistry, finance, logistics, healthcare and security. Published benchmarks up to 2025 are normalized to common metrics and augmented by reproducible simulations. Surface-code simulations at the circuit level show that the threshold is around 0.7-1.0%, and the error-suppression factor increases from 1.6 to 11 when the physical error rate is reduced from 0.6% to 0.1%. UCCSD-VQE reproduces H₂ precisely but misses chemical accuracy for a stretched H₄ chain (5.2 mHa), and a 48-CNOT compilation fails it already at 0.01% two-qubit error. For MaxCut on 3-regular graphs, the QAOA depth required to beat Goemans-Williamson rounding increases from 4 qubits to 6 qubits. The asymptotic decoy-state BB84 reaches 1.5 Mb s−1 over 100 km, whereas the twin-field protocols beat the repeaterless bound beyond 280 km. So, physical fidelity and fault tolerance are still the limiting factors for broad quantum advantage, not qubit count. These comparisons also inform computational decision-making by relating algorithm selection to solution quality, physical error rates, and resource constraints. They provide a basis for assessing where quantum optimization may complement established classical methods in practical decision-support applications.

title: Quantum machine learning for quantitative finance
authors: Piotr Mironowicz, Akshata Shenoy H., Antonio Mandarino, A Ege Yilmaz, Thomas Ankenbrand
abstract: Machine learning (ML) and quantum ML (QML) have gained significant importance, as they offer powerful tools for tackling complex computational problems across various domains. An overview of QML’s uses in quantitative finance is presented here. The connection between quantum computing and ML in financial applications, spanning a range of use cases including portfolio optimization, market prediction and trading, pricing and risk management is examined. The different applications from the literature review are categorized based on specific use cases, ML approaches, optimization methods, and the types of quantum hardware utilized. To facilitate this examination, we employ a morphological box, which allows us to analyze different combinations of these elements across financial use cases.

title: Wave-based dispatch for circuit cutting in hybrid HPC–quantum systems
authors: Ricard Santiago Raigada García, Josep Jorba, Sergio Iserte
abstract: Hybrid High-performance Computing (HPC)—quantum workloads based on circuit cutting decompose large quantum circuits into independent fragments, but existing frameworks tightly couple cutting logic to execution orchestration, preventing HPC centers from applying mature resource management policies to Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) workloads. We present DQR (Dynamic Queue Router) , a runtime framework that bridges this gap by treating circuit fragments as first-class schedulable units. The framework introduces a backend-agnostic fragment descriptor to expose structural properties without requiring execution layers to parse quantum code, a wave-based coordinator that achieves pipeline concurrency via non-blocking polling, and a production-ready implementation on the CESGA Qmio supercomputer integrating both QPUs local on-premises (Qmio) and remote cloud (IBM Torino) backends. Experiments on a 32-qubit Hardware-Efficient Ansatz (HEA) circuit demonstrate not only makespan improvements over a monolithic CPU baseline but also transparent per-fragment failover recovery —specifically rerouting tasks from the local QPU to classical simulators upon encountering hardware–level incompatibilities—without pipeline restart. For deeper circuits, the coordination residual accounts for only 5% of the total execution time, highlighting the framework’s scalability. These results show that DQR enables HPC centers to integrate NISQ workloads into existing production infrastructure while preserving the flexibility to adopt improved cutting algorithms or heterogeneous backend technologies.

title: Simulation-based hybrid quantum–classical QAOA–QWS heuristic for tourist–scenic spot–ICH ternary matching in rural cultural tourism
authors: Jing Wang, Jing Ha
abstract: Rural cultural tourism resource allocation requires coordinated matching among tourist preferences, scenic spot capacities, and intangible cultural heritage (ICH) project services, forming a constrained high-dimensional ternary matching problem. This study develops QAOA-QWS, a simulation-based hybrid quantum–classical heuristic that combines the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) with Quantum Walk Search (QWS). A sparse candidate-triplet representation is first constructed, after which the exact-assignment and resource-capacity constraints are incorporated into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization formulation and mapped to an Ising-type cost Hamiltonian. QAOA performs blockwise low-energy sampling, and QWS subsequently refines the measured candidate subspace through energy-selective marking and graph-dependent quantum-walk evolution. Across five problem scales, QAOA-QWS achieves the highest mean normalized objective value among QAOA only, QUBO-SA, Tabu Search, and genetic algorithms. On the largest instance, it obtains a normalized objective value of 0.869 ± 0.022, a low-energy feasible sampling ratio of 60.5 ± 3.9%, and a post-procedure feasible-state ratio of 90.8 ± 2.2%. Under a separate common fixed-wall-clock protocol, QAOA-QWS retains the highest objective value on all scales and achieves 0.866 ± 0.022 on the largest instance. On the tractable S1 and S2 instances, its gaps to the exact MILP optima are 1.71% and 2.16%, respectively. Sensitivity analyses further show trade-offs between utility preservation and constraint enforcement under different weight and penalty settings. These results support QWS-based candidate-subspace refinement within the tested circuit-simulation setting.

title: Imaginary-time-enhanced feedback-based quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation
authors: Thanh Nguyen Van Long, Lan Nguyen Tran, Le Bin Ho
abstract: Preparing ground states of strongly correlated quantum systems is a central goal in quantum simulation and optimization. The feedback-based quantum algorithm (FALQON) provides an attractive alternative to variational methods with a fully quantum feedback rule, but it fails in the presence of spectral degeneracies, where the feedback signal collapses and the evolution cannot reach the ground state. Using the Fermi-Hubbard model on lattices up to 3 × 3, we show that this breakdown appears at half filling on the 2 × 2 lattice and extends to both half-filled and doped configurations on the 3 × 3 lattice. We then introduce an imaginary-time-enhanced FALQON (i FALQON) scheme, which inserts short imaginary-time evolution steps into the feedback loop. This proposed method suppresses excited-state components, escapes degenerate subspaces, restores monotonic energy descent, and improves ground-state convergence across the tested fillings. We further benchmark its performance against existing methods, showing improved results for i FALQON, demonstrating the potential of hybrid real-imaginary-time feedback dynamics for ground-state preparation in strongly correlated quantum systems.

title: Physics‐Informed Quantum Machine Learning with Hard Constraint Embedding for Nonlinear Differential Equations of the First Order
authors: Mengke Xu, Xi Li, Xiao Chen, Xunan Wang, Wanli Huo, Long Ma, Weiqi Yan
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on linear‐system approaches for solving differential equations demand qubit and precision resources beyond near‐term capabilities. To address these challenges, this work proposes a physics‐informed quantum machine learning (PIQML) framework with hard constraint embedding, designed for NISQ era. Within this framework, parameterized quantum circuits serve as machine learning models, where the input variable is encoded into a high‐dimensional feature space via a Fourier feature map. Subsequently, to eliminate approximation errors in critical physical conditions, the solution is constructed through a rigorously designed function mapper that analytically enforces initial conditions as hard constraints. Crucially, we compute derivatives with respect to the input variable using the parameter‐shift rule—a quantum native gradient evaluation technique that avoids classical discretization. Unlike generic loss functions that target abstract data patterns, our loss function focuses on the differential equation residual and reference data. This design ensures that the trained model not only approximates the data but also intrinsically satisfies the physical constraint expressed by the DE itself. Our method is validated on several differential equations, including highly oscillatory ones, demonstrating its capability to tackle challenging nonlinear dynamics. Results demonstrate that our quantum model learns the solution, showing close agreement with a high‐precision classical numerical benchmark.

title: Accelerating noisy variational quantum algorithms with physics-informed denoising networks
authors: Jie Liu, Xin Wang
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are promising for near-term quantum computing, but are severely limited by hardware noise and the substantial circuit overhead required for error mitigation methods such as Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE). We propose a Physics-Informed Denoising Network (PIDN) that reduces the cost of ZNE by learning a surrogate model of its optimization dynamics. By viewing the variational update as a trajectory in the parameter space, PIDN is trained to reproduce ZNE-mitigated expectation values and gradient directions while incorporating a physics-informed loss that preserves the gradient descent dynamics. Once trained, PIDN replaces repeated multi-noise evaluations with denoised expectation and gradient estimation directly from the current noisy observation and the historical trajectory, significantly reducing circuit executions. We benchmark the approach on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm for 3-regular graphs, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, and transverse-field Ising models, as well as the variational quantum eigensolver for LiH, BeH2 and H2O. Across all tasks, PIDN attains performance comparable to ZNE, while reducing the number of circuit executions by a factor of approximately 4 to 6. Gradient cosine similarity with ZNE remains above 0.95 throughout training. Robustness analysis shows that PIDN fails only when ZNE itself becomes unreliable, and ablation studies confirm the necessity of the physics-informed loss for maintaining directional consistency. We further find that PIDN tracks optimization dynamics most accurately when the effective loss landscape retains strong low-frequency structure. These results establish PIDN as a scalable, resource-efficient strategy for noise-resilient variational optimization in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum regime.

title: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for a Frustrated Ising Model: Simulations and Quantum‐Hardware Experiments
authors: Seunghan Lee, Hunpyo Lee
abstract: A frustrated Ising model on a two‐dimensional square lattice is investigated using exact diagonalization and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with additional benchmarks on IonQ quantum hardware. The dependence of the ground‐state sampling probability on the number of QAOA layers and the frustration strength is analyzed. In weakly frustrated regimes, the probability increases rapidly with a modest increase in the number of QAOA layers. In contrast, in the strongly frustrated regime, the probability remains limited even at larger circuit depths, reflecting the enhanced degeneracy and low‐energy competition induced by frustration. This behavior indicates that strongly frustrated, nearly degenerate regimes present a greater challenge for finite‐depth QAOA. Hardware‐oriented tests are also performed in the non‐frustrated regime, where ideal QAOA simulations reproduce the exact result. On a noisy simulator and IonQ quantum hardware, however, the probability decreases as the number of layers increases, showing that hardware noise still limits the achievable performance of deeper QAOA circuits.
